articles.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
articles.summary: The appointment was made after it emerged Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom By Kali Hays ,  Technology reporter   and   Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent 
- Published 10 November 2026 
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy. 
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. 
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe . 
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday. 
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. 
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. 
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. 
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. 
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. 
- 
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
- Published 1 day ago 
- 
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
- Published 4 days ago 
According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. 
Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". 
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. 
However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. 
The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. 
When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. 
It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. 
Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. 
The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. 
He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. 
It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. 
A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

articles.title: What we know as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over affair allegations
articles.summary: The billionaire tech executive has left the company following reports of a second extramarital affair.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation By Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent   and   Peter Hoskins ,  Business reporter 
- Published 9 November 2026 Updated 12 November 2026 
One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. 
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. 
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. 
Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. 
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. 
- 
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy 
How was Huang removed? 
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. 
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. 
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. 
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". 
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. 
Who will replace him? 
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . 
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. 
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. 
Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. 
And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. 
What we know about Huang's affairs 
A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing. 
She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. 
The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". 
Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. 
She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event 
Who is Jensen Huang? 
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the west coast of the US. 
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. 
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. 
Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. 
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. 
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. 
At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Who is Alice Huang? 
US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . 
She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. 
Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. 
However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. 
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. 
It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. 
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. 
China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". 
- 
Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy 
- Published 3 days ago 
- 
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
- Published 4 days ago 
- 
Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair 
- Published 3 days ago 
Why does it matter? 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small. 
The firm is also at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among US lawmakers. 
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. 
The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. 
Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. 
This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. 
He has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. 
The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House 
What investigations are now under way? 
After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. 
It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now a litigation partner at the law firm. 
US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the scandal, adding that Huang told him he had been unaware the woman he was with was a spy. 
Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November, but has yet to say he will comply. 
What is Nvidia and how important is it? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
There is no clear successor for Jensen Huang at Nvidia 
Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for gaming. 
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates . 
Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. 
He bet on AI at a time when "there were no customers for the stuff he was building", Witt told the BBC. 
Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure like Amazon, Google and Microsoft now use Nvidia chips. 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world. 
Who is Jensen Huang's wife? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Lori Huang and her husband at a state dinner by Trump for his Chinese President Xi Jinping 
Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. 
They married in 1985 and have two children, Madison and Spencer. 
Earlier this week, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. 
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. 
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. 
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him." 
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. 
"But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." 
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

articles.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
articles.summary: Thousands of messages seen by BBC show how a Chinese official sought details of sensitive political matters.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested him By Joe Pike ,  politics investigations correspondent   and   Phil Kemp ,  politics reporter 
- Published 11 November 2026 
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map". 
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister. 
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official. 
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role. 
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved. 
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence. 
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security. 
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China. 
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party. 
Image source, Chris Cash Image caption, 
Chris Cash, left, and Chris Berry met in 2018 when they were teaching in China 
With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others. 
Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media". 
He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources. 
Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with". 
He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster. 
Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government. 
Inside the China Spy Case 
The espionage row that rocked Westminster 
Listen on Sounds 
- 
Watch: Inside the China Spy Case on the BBC News YouTube channel , external 
UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state. 
England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time. 
This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government. 
China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander". 
'A psychological game of chess' 
The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation". 
In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China. 
In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything." 
Figure caption, 
Listen: Berry tells Cash about his invitation to meet a senior Chinese official 
Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound. 
The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says. 
He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea." 
Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing". 
At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win. 
Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question. 
"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash. 
After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now". 
In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state. 
But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party". 
The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet". 
"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact." 
'Bigger deal than I thought' 
So who was the mystery official Berry had met? 
"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought." 
Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Berry identified Cai Qi (left) as the man he had met - a trusted aide of Chinese President Xi Jinping 
Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi. 
What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system. 
For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really." 
We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us. 
Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says. 
Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked. 
Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together". 
The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said. 
At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary. 
He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026. 
Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy? 
Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK. 
He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster. 
The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch. 
It was to be their final face-to-face conversation. 
'Complete shock' 
Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh. 
"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says. 
"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical." 
Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London. 
Chris Berry was also arrested the same day. 
It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends. 
But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport. 
His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded. 
Berry later messaged Cash about it. 
Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China." 
As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK". 
The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine. 
They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients. 
According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents. 
Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily. 
The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy. 
Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function. 
Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it. 
But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on. 
Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work". 
One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities. 
Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues. 
Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says. 
Acquitted and 'traduced' 
Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life. 
But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament. 
Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up." 
Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage. 
In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor. 
"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges." 
His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story. 
Image caption, 
Cash's life has changed almost beyond recognition, he says, but he is positive about the future 
At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing. 
Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life." 
It wouldn't be that simple. 
Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated." 
There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up." 
"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible." 
Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

articles.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
articles.summary: The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy By Tessa Wong   and   Osmond Chia ,  Reporting from Singapore 
- Published 3 hours ago 
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. 
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. 
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets. 
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years. 
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns. 
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. 
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips. 
Megaspeed is a case in point. 
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. 
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. 
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. 
The city-state has had some success in policing this. 
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places. 
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Megaspeed's office in Singapore 
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore. 
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere. 
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed. 
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department. 
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. 
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months. 
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case. 
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing. 
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times. 
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses. 
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. 
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". 
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting 
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness. 
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively. 
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law. 
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities. 
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case. 
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road. 
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed. 
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. 
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS. 
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences. 
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023 
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore. 
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said. 
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore". 
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips. 
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts. 
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China. 
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said. 
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said. 
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China". 
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

articles.title: Eurovision is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up to take the stage
articles.summary: On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
Mongolia's Beck debuted as a singer in 2007 and has since made his mark in acting, hosting, modelling and producing By Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent ,  Reporting from Bangkok 
- Published 6 hours ago 
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory. 
Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year. 
And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia. 
It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts. 
Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT). 
Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region. 
"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust. 
"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer. 
"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly." 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
MANG x DAOU have winning form, having previously been declared champions of the show Thailand's Chosen One 
Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars. 
This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through. 
Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan. 
Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one. 
There have also been problems with the organisation of this event. 
A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too. 
Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Eurovision is coming to Asia - but will it succeed? 
The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category. 
Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others. 
The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points". 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
JUNHEE is a solo singer-songwriter from South Korea who produces bright, mainstream-sounding music 
In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote. 
Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool. 
For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before. 
"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us." 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
Nyendra, Bhutan's 24-year-old contestant, is also a journalism graduate 
The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format – no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music. 
This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience – think Poland's My Słowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry. 
There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh – where same-sex activity is illegal – and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year. 
Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers. 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
Thinla's music blends traditional Lao and contemporary genres, such as pop, R&B and dance 
Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer Tóc Tiên's song Em Tiên ("Fairy Maiden"). 
It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time. 
The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music. 
The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth. 
"I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us. 
"The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are." 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
Bangladesh's Beatmosphere blend traditional vocal harmony with beatbox culture 
Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, 
Carmelle Collado rose to prominence through a selection of televised singing competitions in the Philippines 
Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988. 
Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets. 
Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest. 
Image caption, 
Malaysia's Aina Abdul laughs as designer Melinda Looi adjusts her dress before a media shoot 
Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water. 
If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.

articles.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s company aborted an attempted catch of the rocket’s booster - instead it came down in the ocean.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean as it burst into flames By Rebecca Morelle ,  Science Editor   and   Alison Francis ,  Senior science journalist 
- Published 13 November 2026 Updated 1 hour ago 
SpaceX aborted its attempt to catch the bottom part of its huge Starship rocket during its latest test flight. 
The aim was to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth, but instead it was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames as it came down. 
The top part of the rocket is now continuing its journey to space, and SpaceX will decide whether it will try to catch this rocket stage - at about 1515 local time (2115 GMT) on Saturday. 
It's the company's first attempt to fully recover its rocket, paving the way for making Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs. 
Image source, SpaceX Image caption, 
Starship is the tallest and most powerful rocket ever built 
The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) on Friday. 
It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean. 
During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely." 
The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space. 
The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted. 
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. 
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean. 
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space. 
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean. 
Image source, SpaceX Image caption, 
A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon 
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX. 
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster. 
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch. 
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society. 
"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said. 
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate." 
- 
What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next? 
- Published 27 October 
- 
Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test 
- Published 28 September 
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency. 
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline. 
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface. 
But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down. 
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule. 
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers. 
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended. 
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida. 
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027. 
Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.summary: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.
articles.full_text:
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
Putin sounded uncompromising and confident at his talks with the US envoys By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,  Reporting from Moscow 
- Published 9 hours ago 
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine. 
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire. 
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace? 
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace." 
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia. 
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War. 
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. 
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin. 
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia". 
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them. 
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow. 
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week. 
"Our proposals were almost laughed at. 
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement." 
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire". 
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture." 
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table. 
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia. 
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US. 
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks. 
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken. 
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

And what of Putin? 
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident. 
You can see why. 
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him. 
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe. 
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield. 
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure. 
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages. 
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
articles.summary: Scott Bessent suggests Howard Lutnick’s commerce department failed to ban exports of Nvidia's chips to a firm thought to have links with China.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? By Rachel Clun ,  Business Reporter ,  Reporting from New York   and   Bernd Debusmann, Jr ,  White House reporter 
- Published 13 November 2026 
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. 
Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. 
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. 
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. 
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". 
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. 
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. 
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed 
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. 
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. 
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. 
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. 
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. 
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme , external . 
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? 
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." 
Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. 
In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media.

Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. 
The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. 
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. 
Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang. 
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. 
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection. 
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.

articles.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
articles.summary: German reforms mean foreign and domestic intelligence services will have greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
In future, German spies working for the BND foreign intelligence service will be able to conduct covert operations abroad By Bethany Bell Germany reporter 
- Published 13 November 2026 
Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation. 
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers. 
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police. 
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution. 
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained. 
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it. 
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage. 
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons. 
Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified. 
That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.

- Published 22 October 
-

- Published 8 September 
-

- Published 2 September 
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance. 
They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet. 
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran. 
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers." 
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty. 
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack. 
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police. 
And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of". 
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era. 
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers." 
However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

articles.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? By Michelle Fleury 
New York business correspondent 
- Published 13 November 2026 
How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang? 
The answer is very. 
The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China. 
Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China. 
Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities. 
But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country. 
Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits. 
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated. 
Image source, Getty Images 
The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. 
US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it? 
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. 
His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. 
On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections. 
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. 
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. 
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist. 
On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". 
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. 
There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department. 
This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle. 
Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach. 
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure. 
Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips. 
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open. 
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors. 
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment. 
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history". 
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out. 
There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long? 
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump. 
The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns. 
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department. 
Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action
US commerce secretary faces sack as questions emerge over senior Trump officials’ knowledge of alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang 
- 
US politics – live updates 
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions. 
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China. 
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the company’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress , after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. 
White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration . 
Lutnick is now scheduled to testify before Congress next month, just days after the ousted Nvidia chief answers lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill. 
Lutnick is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration. 
Bessent has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added in an interview with the network on Friday. 
View image in fullscreen 
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, on 22 May 2025. Photograph: CTI/AFPTV/AFP/Getty Images 
John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”. 
The Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times that there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls”, adding: “Heads should roll.” A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang 
Read more 
The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether US security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang. 
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News. 
Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge . The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported . 
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images 
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia. 
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, citing “recent reports [that] raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology”. The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal-conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded. 
Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters. 
The House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony. 
View image in fullscreen 
The Taiwan Stock Exchange opened 627.88 points higher on Friday, at 43,719.75, with a turnover of 21.86bn New Taiwan dollars ($662.87m), amid uncertainty in the AI sector. Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPA 
The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China . 
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them. 
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“ 
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters . 
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models. 
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday. 
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as Huang’s swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for more than three decades. 
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo. 
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
